title: Binance Pay Opens Crypto Payments at Millions of PayPay Merchants Across Japan
summary:
Key Takeaways: Binance Pay is now available for visitors to use at PayPay merchants in Japan. Crypto is immediately converted to JPY. The Binance Pay tourist users have increased by
The post Binance Pay Opens Crypto Payments at Millions of PayPay Merchants Across Japan appeared first on CryptoNinjas...
content:
Key Takeaways:

  • Binance Pay is now available for visitors to use at PayPay merchants in Japan.
  • Crypto is immediately converted to JPY.
  • The Binance Pay tourist users have increased by 20% between July and August 2026.

Binance is expanding crypto payments in Japan through a new integration between Binance Pay and PayPay, one of the country’s largest QR payment networks.

It provides features which allow eligible tourists to use the crypto payments at the millions of stores supported by PayPay without a prior exchange of yen or sign up for a local payment account.

  • Binance Pay Connects Crypto to Japan’s PayPay Network
  • Stablecoins and Major Crypto Assets Can Fund Payments
    • Binance Pay Tourist Activity Jumps 20%
    • Japan Expands Binance Pay’s Asian QR Footprint

Binance Pay Connects Crypto to Japan’s PayPay Network

Japan is also allowing tourists to pay using crypto in the local retail market while they are travelling the country using their Binance account balance.

A merchant can have a code to open Binance Pay at checkout, and paykey can read the code to complete the transaction. For some stores, visitors can also scan the store’s PayPay QR and type the amount of the purchase.

The crypto currency is converted in real time to the JPY units and the merchant gets the local currency. That’s no longer a problem because travelers can use digital assets without having to sell them for JPY first or withdraw cash.

The feature is accessible just for tourists to Japan who are Binance ID verified customers. Not usable to Japanese people.

Read More: Binance Bitcoin Outflows Hit 13,800 BTC in 3-Year Record as FOMO Returns

Stablecoins and Major Crypto Assets Can Fund Payments

According to Binance’s description of its QR payment network, Binance Pay currently lets people pay for travel with assets like USDT, USDC, BTC, BNB and ETH.

The payment system will also perform the translation from crypto to fiat with checkout, so that all users still have the same purchasing process in every country.

Additionally, Binance claims that users are not charged any blockchain gas fees when making these payments via Binance Pay.

The solution simplifies the solution for travellers who would otherwise need to spend local currency first or make a separate wallet beforehand to send and receive crypto during travel.

Binance Pay Tourist Activity Jumps 20%

Binance has noted that there is an increasing trend of tourists using cryptocurrencies, with active users rising 20% from July to August 2026.

Japan becomes another market where the firm is expanding its payments with QR code business across Asia.

Instead of creating a new merchant network, Binance Pay integrates with the local payment ecosystem, allowing merchants to seamlessly utilize the QR codes already in use at their physical locations.

The same idea has been used in Vietnam as well, by integrating VietQR for tourists to pay with crypto while local fiat is paid to merchants.

Read More: Binance Wallet Opens $4.7T Pre-IPO Market Access Through PancakeSwap Tokenized Deals

Japan Expands Binance Pay’s Asian QR Footprint

PayPay provides Binance Pay with a vast network of merchants in convenient stores, restaurants and other common venues spread throughout Japan.

The integration is for bitcoin customers to spend cryptocurrencies the same way they spend money, rather than via a whole separate blockchain payment. Binance will roll out this model to other Asia-Pacific and other markets where QR payment is already popular.

The company is focusing on markets with strong tourist traffic and established QR infrastructure, allowing travelers to use one Binance Pay account across multiple destinations without changing their payment setup each time.

title: Morgan Stanley Builds Crypto Lab to Test Stablecoins, Tokenization and DeFi at Scale
summary:
Key Takeaways: Morgan Stanley has opened a Digital Asset Lab dedicated to blockchain technologies. The test is to be applied to the stablecoins, the tokenized assets and DeFi applications. This
The post Morgan Stanley Builds Crypto Lab to Test Stablecoins, Tokenization and DeFi at Scale appeared fir...
content:
Key Takeaways:

  • Morgan Stanley has opened a Digital Asset Lab dedicated to blockchain technologies.
  • The test is to be applied to the stablecoins, the tokenized assets and DeFi applications.
  • This lab allows employees to try things that they don’t want to do to the bank’s core systems.

Morgan Stanley has given its crypto research a boost with a new blockchain lab, dedicated to joining blockchain-based infrastructure into its financial business toolkit.

The initiative gives the Wall Street bank a controlled environment to study digital money, tokenized products and decentralized finance tools before considering wider deployment.

  • Morgan Stanley Tests Stablecoins and Tokenized Finance
  • DeFi Vaults Join the Testing List
    • Crypto Research Builds on Existing Products
    • Wall Street Pushes Deeper Into Blockchain Infrastructure

Morgan Stanley Tests Stablecoins and Tokenized Finance

The new lab will focus on blockchain based financial infrastructure and stablecoins, tokenized deposits, central bank digital currencies and tokenized money-market funds.

Morgan Stanley is also looking at deFi apps that might find their way into automating financial activity outside normal market hours.

A specific area of interest is how software-based systems can continuously handle investment strategies, with transactions recorded on the blockchain and investment rules executed as they are generated.

The lab will be part of Morgan Stanley’s existing innovation labs. Staff have the opportunity to trial new technology in a testing environment, minimising the impact on the bank’s primary systems.

Read More: South Korea Targets 2027 Tokenized Securities Launch with Stablecoin Settlement Vision

DeFi Vaults Join the Testing List

Another technology that is being considered is DeFi vaults. A smart contract could automate investment strategies or asset management functions as per programmed conditions within these systems. Morgan Stanley is investigating the possibility of combining the model with the standard available financial products.

The bank also plans to examine the differences between tokenized bank deposits and stablecoins. Unlike stablecoins which are backed by a different reserve asset, tokenized deposits are a claim against money that is held by a bank.

It is hoped that learning how both models can fit within institutional finance will be an integral aspect of the lab’s tasks.

Crypto Research Builds on Existing Products

Morgan Stanley is not entering digital assets from scratch. It already hosts Bitcoin, Ether and Solana on its E*TRADE platform for eligible clients and has also introduced cryptocurrency-based investment products.

The bank took the stablecoin industry in its stride too. The Morgan Stanley Investment Management government money-market portfolio was launched partly for the purpose of using it to hold a reserve of stablecoins.

That product focuses on reserve assets such as cash, short-term U.S. Treasurys and Treasury-backed repurchase agreements.

The new Digital Asset Lab is for a different purpose. It’s not another product on the market, It’s a test about how blockchain can be applied to financial operations.

Read More: Cloudflare Unveils Stablecoin Monetization Gateway, Unlocking Instant x402 Payments for Any API

Wall Street Pushes Deeper Into Blockchain Infrastructure

As major financial institutions show increased interest in tokenization of assets and blockchain settlement systems, Morgan Stanley’s research echoes the trend.

The bank is also exploring the banks of digital finance, from the underlying infrastructure of the system, like blockchain-based programmable assets and automated investment services, to custody.

For its part, the financial firm’s proposed trust platform is said to be part of Morgan Stanley’s plans to launch a crypto infrastructure, including custody and services provided by outside parties.

For now, the technologies being tested in the Digital Asset Lab remain experimental. Products such as tokenized deposits and DeFi vaults are research areas rather than services currently available to Morgan Stanley clients.

title: Trezor Cuts Resellers After $86M Wallet Tampering Scare, Says Devices Remain Safe
summary:
Key Takeaways: Trezor recently has seen hardware wallet supply chain issues, so it has shortened its list of authorized retailers. According to the company, no proof of any trespass on
The post Trezor Cuts Resellers After $86M Wallet Tampering Scare, Says Devices Remain Safe appeared first on Crypto...
content:
Key Takeaways:

  • Trezor recently has seen hardware wallet supply chain issues, so it has shortened its list of authorized retailers.
  • According to the company, no proof of any trespass on any Trezor devices.
  • This stems from a recent news report on malicious hardware implants being discovered in Ledger hardware from a reseller.

Trezor is bolstering its supply chain of hardware wallets, reducing the number of resellers authorized to distribute them. The company said that it is making the decision in anticipation of a breach and not as a result of a confirmed breach of any Trezor product.

Following recent supply-chain incidents, we decided to reduce the number of resellers so we can more effectively check those we work with.

Let us be very clear: there is not a single piece of evidence that Trezor devices have been compromised.

This is a preventive step, taken out of an abundance of caution. We also want to thank everyone involved for the cooperation, and for the years of work putting Trezor in people’s hands.

— Trezor (@Trezor) October 13, 2026

  • Trezor Reduces Reseller Network After Supply-Chain Incidents
  • Trezor Says No Devices Have Been Compromised
    • Hardware Wallet Security Moves Beyond Firmware
    • Users Urged to Check Where Their Wallet Comes From

Trezor Reduces Reseller Network After Supply-Chain Incidents

Trezor says it will engage fewer resellers, in an effort to more closely monitor the partners it is putting its hardware wallet products into the hands of. The firm attributed the action to counter security breaches in the hardware wallet space in the recent past.

Trezor CCO Danny Sanders also announced that some resellers had been notified that they will no longer be part of Trezor’s authorized sellers from 1st January. In addition, affected resellers were also meant to have their shipments stopped.

To the resellers who helped build Trezor: thank you, and I’m sorry 💔 https://t.co/RK7KBJOshp

— Danny (@Dantoshi) October 13, 2026

Trezor thanked its long-term distribution partners in order to extend access to its wallets, and noted that the new policy applies to companies working with the brand for many years.

Read More: Bits of Gold Breach May Expose 200,000 Crypto Users, But Funds Remain Safe Online

Trezor Says No Devices Have Been Compromised

One clear point that was set is that there is no evidence of Trezor hardware wallets being compromised.

The difference is significant, since the resellers belong to a report in which competitor hardware wallet provider Ledger is involved with an illegal hardware installation in at least one wallet.

They reported that it was not a typical attack regarding the firmware modification. Malicious hardware was made so as to collect confidential information for the purpose of recovery, and send it outside of the device.

Existing set-up on Trezor is designed to detect tampering, including counterfeiting, and firmware alteration, but a hardware tampering is a new form of a supply-chain threat.

Hardware Wallet Security Moves Beyond Firmware

The incident marks the scope of a problem afflicting self-custody users in general. Even though hardware wallets have secure, offline characteristics, their security can be influenced by how they move from manufacturer to the customer.

A physically tampered with device could outsmart a device that protects primarily against changes in the instruction set software or the firmware. That’s why, instead of making any announcement regarding the wallets, Trezor is putting more focus on reseller supervision.

Read More: Bitget Halts Withdrawals After $351.6M Hot Wallet Incident Hits Crypto Exchange

Users Urged to Check Where Their Wallet Comes From

Trezor has recommended its users to buy devices from the company if at all possible and ensure the products are intact. Users with larger crypto portfolios are further presented with multisignature setups as an option by the firm.

In the case of multisig, multiple keys are needed to validate a deal, which means that in the event of a compromised device, it will be unable to move funds alone. The reseller reduction, therefore, is a security measure for the supply chain and not a reaction to a confirmed hack on Trezor.

title: Qubic freezes chain after attacker drains 1.4K wallets with weak seeds
summary: Qubic says 87.1% of the stolen funds remain onchain and the rest were frozen at crypto exchange MEXC, as network validators prepare to vote on a recovery plan.
content:
Layer-1 blockchain network Qubic halted operations Sunday after an attacker reportedly exploited weakly generated wallet seeds to drain approximately $1.4 million from more than 1,400 accounts, according to the project. 

In a statement on X, Qubic said the network was halted at tick 85,371,949, where it remains paused at the time of writing. Qubic said the vulnerability affected wallet seeds generated using any browser on an iPhone or iPad, Safari on a Mac until Oct. 18, 2026, or the Qubic iOS app before July 2025, leading to 2.94 trillion Qubit (QU) stolen. 

“87.1% of the drained funds never left the Qubic network and remain frozen in place,” said Qubic. “The remaining 12.9% was sent to MEXC, whose team froze the receiving account within about an hour.” 

The Qubic theft is the latest in a series of attacks tied to weak wallet seeds. In July, Coldcard disclosed that attackers had stolen funds from wallets whose seeds were weakened by a firmware bug. Similar flaws affected Trust Wallet’s browser extension and the Libbitcoin Explorer tool in 2023.

Related: Bitget’s $388M hack pushes Q3 crypto security losses past $1B

Qubic said it has fixed the seed-generation flaw in the latest version of its web wallet. 

A GitHub commit for version 4.26.4 shows that Qubic replaced JavaScript’s Math.random() function, which is not suitable for generating cryptographic secrets, with the cryptographically secure crypto.getRandomValues() function when creating wallet seeds. 

Qubic said its core team is identifying affected wallets and preparing recovery options for a vote by the network’s Computors, which will decide what happens to the frozen funds. The team said it would publish a full technical report after a recovery plan is settled. It has not announced when the network will restart.

Qubic did not immediately respond to Cointelegraph’s request for comment. 

Qubic is a layer-1 blockchain that supports transactions and smart contracts without fees. It is built on Useful Proof of Work (UPoW) – a consensus mechanism that repurposes mining energy to train artificial intelligence. Qubic’s token had a market capitalization of about $62.6 million at the time of writing, according to CoinGecko.

In the third quarter, hacks and exploits accounted for 19% of crypto crime cases but 40% of reported losses, according to AMLBot’s 2026 investigations report, which looked at 250 investigations it opened since the start of the year.

title: Wall Street Braces for Black Monday’s Return 39 Years Later
summary: Thirty-nine years after Wall Street’s worst single-day percentage collapse, the calendar is playing a familiar trick. Oct. 19 falls on a Monday again, just as oil tops $100, artificial intelligence stocks buckle, and inflation rattles investors. Social media is sounding the Black Monday alarm, but t...
content:
Thirty-nine years after Wall Street’s worst single-day percentage collapse, the calendar is playing a familiar trick. Oct. 19 falls on a Monday again, just as oil tops $100, artificial intelligence stocks buckle, and inflation rattles investors. Social media is sounding the Black Monday alarm, but the parallels with 1987 come with important differences, including safeguards designed to prevent another historic market rout.

Key Takeaways

  • The Dow plunged 22.6% on Oct. 19, 1987, and its 39th anniversary falls on another Monday.
  • Oil above $100, AI stock losses and inflation have revived Black Monday fears across Wall Street.
  • Bitcoin has held near $82,000, while U.S. stock market circuit breakers provide safeguards absent in 1987.

Wall Street’s Black Monday Ghost Returns as Oil, AI, and Inflation Rattle Markets

Wall Street has a date with an old nightmare. On Monday, Oct. 19, 2026, the 39th anniversary of the infamous 1987 Black Monday crash arrives with stocks battered, oil above $100 a barrel and investors increasingly nervous about the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.

The original catastrophe erased 22.6% from the Dow Jones Industrial Average in a single trading session, a record that still stands. Now, with technology shares taking a beating and inflation refusing to cooperate, social media is drawing comparisons to that historic financial calamity. But does the market actually resemble 1987, or is Wall Street chasing ghosts?

“Calls for a ‘Black Monday’ are spreading rapidly across social media right now,” The Kobeissi Letter wrote on X on Saturday. “If history is any guide, this means the S&P 500 should hit 8,000 soon. Ignore the noise.”

The 1987 Anniversary Meets a Bruised Stock Market

The coincidence is enough to raise eyebrows. On Oct. 19, 1987, the Dow suffered its worst one-day percentage decline, wiping approximately $500 billion from U.S. equity valuations. Automated trading and portfolio insurance strategies amplified the selling, transforming market weakness into a full-blown rout. Thirty-nine years later, the anniversary falls on precisely the same weekday.

“Black Monday is tomorrow,” the X account known as MBAeconomics told his 18,700 followers. “Stocks will crash. Hopefully, you have dry powder ready to buy the dip in precious metals and mining stocks. In environments like this, gold outperforms everything.”

Friday’s trading provided fresh ammunition for the doomsayers. The S&P 500 finished Oct. 16 at 7,659.44, down 1.09%, while the Nasdaq Composite lost approximately 2.2%. Artificial intelligence-related companies bore much of the punishment. Coreweave dropped nearly 12% in Friday’s session as investors questioned the economics of enormous AI infrastructure commitments.

“WARNING: TOMORROW WILL BE THE WORST BLACK MONDAY IN HISTORY,” the social media account Cryptonobler said to his 389,800 X followers. “98% of people will lose everything. Markets have officially entered panic mode.” Cryptonobler added:

“For the first time EVER, something just broke in the economy. If you hold any assets today, you MUST read this before October 19: When markets open on Monday, this won’t be just a routine correction. What is happening right now is anything BUT normal.”

Oil Above $100 and Inflation Put the Fed in a Bind

Energy markets have thrown another wrench into Wall Street’s calculations. Brent crude approached $110 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate traded above $100 amid geopolitical tensions involving Iran, the Strait of Hormuz, and attacks on energy infrastructure. Higher energy costs threaten to complicate inflation further. September’s consumer price index reportedly reached 3.7% annually, while the Federal Reserve’s September rate increase placed its benchmark target between 3.75% and 4%.

Meanwhile, the Cboe Volatility Index, commonly called the VIX, climbed toward 20 as investors paid more for protection against market turbulence. The combination recalls some of 1987’s underlying pressures, particularly elevated valuations, interest-rate anxiety and concerns about excessive financial leverage.

AI Stocks Take a Beating as Gold and Bitcoin Hold Their Ground

AI, previously a principal engine of stock market enthusiasm, has become a source of financial unease. Coreweave’s recent weakness reflects mounting questions about borrowing costs, infrastructure spending, and whether future AI revenues can justify today’s enormous investments. Some of the company’s debt reportedly approached yields of 15%, reflecting heightened concerns about financing risks.

Elsewhere, gold traded around $4,150 to $4,200 per ounce, while silver hovered near $56 to $58. Bitcoin’s price, meanwhile, changed hands around $80,400 to $81,000 over the weekend, displaying relative stability compared with Friday’s technology-sector losses. The broader cryptocurrency market stood near $2.7 trillion. That resilience offers little guarantee against a wider liquidation event, particularly if investors begin selling liquid assets to cover losses elsewhere.

Wall Street Has Safeguards That Didn’t Exist in 1987

Here’s where the Black Monday comparison runs into trouble. Modern U.S. stock exchanges operate market-wide circuit breakers that interrupt trading when the S&P 500 falls 7% or 13%. A 20% decline triggers a trading halt for the remainder of the session. Those protections emerged from the lessons of 1987 and subsequent market disruptions.

Today’s selling also remains concentrated in technology rather than spreading uniformly across the financial system. Still, elevated borrowing costs, expensive energy and heavily financed AI projects represent genuine vulnerabilities. Still, not everyone is buying the bearish rumors. For instance, one individual on X wrote:

“Black Monday never happens when 99% of people expect it.”

The anniversary itself predicts nothing. Yet Wall Street enters Monday facing an uncomfortable question. If the AI investment boom starts losing its financial footing, who gets stuck footing the bill?

title: SEC tokenized stock framework faces issuer pushback as Broadcom, Verizon object to OKX-ICE listing
summary: Eight more companies objected to trading on the planned OKX-ICE venue, while Nasdaq has separately said it would opt out under the SEC’s framework.
content:
Oct 18, 2026, 7:28 p.m. EDT

2 min read

Summary

  • Broadcom, Verizon and UnitedHealth are among nine companies objecting to having their shares traded on OKXICE’s planned tokenized-stock platform.
  • The venue would use the SEC’s five-year Innovation Exemption to offer around-the-clock trading of blockchain-based shares backed one-for-one by underlying stock.
  • Issuer resistance and uncertainty over the temporary regulatory framework could limit available stocks and discourage institutional investment in tokenized trading infrastructure.

The SEC’s new framework for trading tokenized stocks is encountering resistance from some of the companies whose shares could trade, with Broadcom (AVGO), Verizon (VZ) and UnitedHealth (UNH) among the latest issuers to object.

Eight newly disclosed objections appeared in an October 15 public notice from OKXICE, the joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) preparing to offer tokenized stock trading.

Alongside Broadcom, Verizon and UnitedHealth, the notice names AppLovin (APP), Applied Digital (APLD), Rocket Lab (RKLB), CoreWeave (CRWV) and Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI).

It lists nine objecting issuers in total, including AI chipmaker Cerebras Systems (CBRS), which formally opted out of being listed earlier. The update did not disclose why the companies objected or when they submitted their notices.

Nasdaq (NDAQ) has separately said it would opt out of having its own shares tokenized under the framework, according to an FAQ on its website.

A Nasdaq spokesperson told the Wall Street Journal that the company does not want its shares trading on a venue that does not display best prices in real time or report to the consolidated tape, which aggregates stock-market trading data. Nasdaq is not among the nine issuers named in OKXICE’s notice.

Path to onchain stock trading

OKXICE announced on October 5 that it had notified the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission of plans to launch the venue, initially targeting shares of 63 U.S.-listed companies. Former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, the venture’s co-chair, announced the move on X.

The venue would operate under the SEC’s five-year “Innovation Exemption,” issued September 17, which allows qualifying platforms to trade tokenized U.S. stocks using automated market makers and liquidity pools.

Tokenized stocks are blockchain-based representations of shares. OKXICE plans to operate around the clock using Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on OKX’s XLayer blockchain, with trades settled in stablecoins.

Under the model described in its notice, underlying shares would be held one-for-one against outstanding tokens through a registered broker-dealer. Token holders must receive equivalent rights, including dividends and voting rights.

Issuer doubts

The issuer pushback echoes findings from TD Securities analysts led by Reid Noch, vice president of U.S. equity market structure.

Conversations with dozens of issuers showed “little interest in tokenizing their shares outside a small group of crypto-adjacent companies,” the analysts wrote in a report shared with CoinDesk. Several issuers also approached the firm with significant concerns after discovering the framework, having been unaware of it when it was announced, the report said.

TD Securities named the framework’s reliance on temporary exemptive relief, rather than permanent rules, as its largest hurdle. A future commission could reverse the approach, complicating the case for investing in infrastructure and discouraging institutions from integrating with venues even after they launch, the analysts said.

That uncertainty is especially challenging when overseas platforms can continue offering synthetic stock products without assuming the operational requirements of the U.S. relief, they added.

title: Richard Heart caught ‘off-guard,’ QDay gets even closer: Hodler’s Digest
summary: HEX founder Richard Heart detained in early morning raid in Istanbul, Starknet plunges almost 50% as it votes to become an L1, and Bitwise says all signs point to Crypto Spring.
content:
HEX erases $246 million in market cap after founder detained in Turkey

The HEX market cap fell from $561 million to $315 million this week after founder Richard Schueler — better known to the crypto community as Richard Heart — was detained by authorities in Istanbul on October 14.

Police seized $7.15 million in cash along with firearms and ammunition during an early morning raid in Istanbul’s Beşiktaş district, alongside searches of 15 related addresses according to Turkish Justice Minister Akın Gürlek.

Police impounded nine luxury vehicles registered to Schueler’s wife according to news agency Anadolu. The haul reportedly included 28 watches, 300 bags and 19 graphics cards.

Interpol issued a “Red Notice” for Schueler’s two years ago over allegations of tax fraud and assault, after Finnish authorities sought his arrest.

A spokesperson for Finland’s National Bureau of Investigations declined to comment on the matter.

Turkish media refer to Schueler as “Whale James” and have linked him to a $1 billion unregistered securities offering in the US. However that case was dismissed by a US judge in February 2025.

Images circulating in Turkish media appear to show a surprised Heart with no trousers on, and the bottom half of his body blurred out, provoking much merriment on social media. Vocal Hex critic Eric Wall, who has debated Schueler on video and social media, said he initially thought the image was AI generated but now believes it is real. (Cointelegraph can only verify the image is circulating not that it has not been altered.)

“i’m pretty much certain i died in a plane crash in 2015 and ever since that day i am still only alive in a fringe reality where everything is designed to be as funny as possible.”

Hex supporters claim that authorities are yet to confirm if Schueler has been formally arrested or charged.

Images circulating on Turkish media.

Ledger’s answer to wallet tampering costs $849 and ships next year

Ledger unveiled a new device on Thursday with stronger protections against tampering, days after confirming that wallets sold through a reseller in Asia contained malicious implants.

The French hardware wallet maker introduced Atom, an $849 device that combines a crypto wallet with everyday apps through a smartphone-like design. Atom separates Android apps from sensitive wallet operations and includes protections Ledger says would block the implants used in the recent Asia incident. It claims to detect tampering even when switched off.

Expected to become available in summer 2027, Atom will also support AI agent approvals, encrypted messaging and post-quantum cryptography.

Meanwhile a war of words has broken out between former Mt Gox CEO Mark Karpeles, and Ledger CEO Pascal Gauthier. Kapeles claims that at least two people notified Leger of spyware discovered inside tampered Ledgers as far back as December 2025 — and notes the company had even written about the issue on its website in March 2026. He says the company failed to act properly to secure its reseller supply chains, which have now been suspended across Asia after more than $90 million was stolen.

Gauthier snarkily replied on X that Karpeles was “no white knight” and referred back to his failures in the lead up to the Mt Gox hack.

Karpeles replied:

“I was hoping you guys were better than that. I’ve been holding Ledger at a higher standard than what happened at MtGox, because I trusted you to do better by learning of my failure — to be better than me.”

QDay gets even closer as Starknet votes on becoming post quantum L1

Google has demonstrated a new process called “magic state cultivation” on its Willow quantum processor that reduces errors 40-fold. The technique achieved a record 99.99% accuracy rate for a specialized quantum state required to perform advanced calculations.

Meanwhile Theta Labs has posted three news quantum circuits that could reduce the number of qubits required to break elliptic curve cryptography by 28% from Google’s current estimate of 1,175 logical qubits.

With fears that AI is now getting so good at math that it may be able to break elliptic curve cryptography even before QDay arrives, Starknet has opened a vote to transform itself from an Ethereum L2 into a post quantum L1. StarkWare CEO Eli Ben-Sasson says that Ethereum’s post quantum roadmap may be too slow to meet the challenge from AI, meaning that Starknet needed to consider becoming a fully post quantum L1.

“Quantum-proofing crypto is urgent, so we must move at lightning speed,” he told Cointelegraph. More than 99% of votes cast to date are in favor of the move. Starknet’s token has lost almost 50% in value this week, after a big surge last week.

Standard Chartered pushes $2T stablecoin forecast to 2030 as EU embraces USDC

Standard Chartered says stablecoin transaction activity continues to grow even as the market’s overall value has stalled, suggesting existing stablecoins are circulating more frequently rather than new supply driving growth.

The bank said it now expects stablecoin market capitalization to reach $2 trillion by 2030, two years later than initially projected, after the market plateaued at roughly $309 billion this year.

Meanwhile the European Banking Authority has classified Circle’s USDC stablecoin as a significant e-money token under the region’s Markets in Crypto Assets (MiCA) framework. The classification has only been granted to 45 projects.

Binance.US seeks $1B valuation in potential $100M funding round

Binance.US reportedly seeks to raise up to $100 million in a funding round that could value the cryptocurrency exchange at $1 billion.

According to a Thursday Bloomberg report, the US-based crypto exchange is pursuing private investment as it looks to expand its business. The potential $1 billion valuation would be well below the $4.5 billion pre-money valuation it secured in 2022, when it raised $200 million in seed funding.

Winners and Losers

At the end of the week, Bitcoin (BTC) is down 3.8% to trade at $81,484, Ethereum (ETH) is down 5.7% to trade at $2,386 and XRP (XRP) is down 8.3% to $1.28. The total market cap is at $2.72 trillion according to CoinMarketCap.

Among the biggest 100 cryptocurrencies, the top three altcoin winners of the week are Monero (XMR) with a 9.7% gain, Injective (INJ) on 5.6%, and Celestia (TIA) on 5.1%.

The top three altcoin losers of the week are Starknet (STRK) which was down 46.7%, Pump.fun (PUMP) down 27.1% and Raydium (RAY) down 26.5%.

Prediction of the Week

Bitwise’s Hougan says Q3 charts point to ‘crypto spring’

Bitwise chief investment officer Matt Hougan says Q3 may have been “one of the best quarters in crypto’s history,” arguing a sharp rebound in crypto prices and growing onchain markets point to the start of “crypto spring.”

In its quarterly market review published Thursday, Bitwise reported a 46.4% quarterly gain in its large-cap crypto index, along with $6 billion in US spot Bitcoin ETF inflows that brought year-to-date net flows back into positive territory. 

“Page after page after page, it’s all the same: The most recent part of the chart is turning sharply upwards,” Hougan wrote. “That’s exactly what you want to see if you’re looking for the start of a crypto spring.”

Top FUD of the Week

MSCI adopts index exclusion rules that could oust Strategy

Index provider MSCI has adopted new rules that could lead to Strategy, Metaplanet and Upexi being removed from its global indexes, while leaving several other crypto treasury companies facing potential exclusion. 

In August, Strategy opposed the changes but also played down the potential disruption, saying funds tracking MSCI’s Global Investable Market Indexes hold approximately 13 million shares, representing 3.1% of its basic shares outstanding. The company said those holdings amount to less than one day’s trading volume.

Russia to ban direct peer-to-peer crypto trades starting July 2027

Russia will ban direct peer-to-peer (P2P) cryptocurrency transactions between individuals starting next year, requiring individuals to use authorized intermediaries for such trades.

The regulator said the ban would come into place on July 1, 2027.

The regulator also clarified that individuals are not allowed to transfer crypto assets from their digital accounts to their own non-custodial, or self-custodial, wallets.

Ex-Trump crypto adviser profited after helping pass stablecoin bill: WSJ

Bo Hines, previously a crypto adviser to US President Donald Trump who later joined stablecoin issuer Tether, reportedly kept a stake in a company that profited from the passage of a stablecoin bill when he was still at the White House.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Hines had a one-third stake in the investment company he co-founded, Nxum, while pushing US lawmakers to pass the GENIUS Act. Nxum reportedly received $6.3 million as part of a deal with stablecoin issuer Tether, with the first payment going through while Hines was still serving in government.

title: Why RWA Tokenization and Onchain Credit Could Boost XRP Demand
summary: Despite XRP’s sharp decline from its mid-2025 peak, institutional adoption and developer activity on the XRP Ledger remain resilient. Odelia Torteman, head of digital assets at XRPL Commons, argues that expanding enterprise use, real-world asset tokenization and upcoming lending features could gener...
content:
Despite XRP’s sharp decline from its mid-2025 peak, institutional adoption and developer activity on the XRP Ledger remain resilient. Odelia Torteman, head of digital assets at XRPL Commons, argues that expanding enterprise use, real-world asset tokenization and upcoming lending features could generate sustainable demand for XRP.

Key Takeaways

  • XRPL Commons’ Odelia Torteman cited $2B RLUSD market cap and top-3 RWA ranking as drivers of institutional adoption.
  • XRPL Commons is partnering with AWS and Mastercard for its 2025 New York hackathon to incubate emerging startups.
  • XRP briefly dipped under $1 in 2026, but institutional adoption from SBI Group reinforces its long-term viability.

Protocol Architecture Drives Core Demand

The convergence of Ripple Labs’ favorable 2023 court decision and the broader regulatory tailwinds of a pro-crypto Trump administration fueled a powerful bull run, propelling XRP to an all-time high in mid-2025. However, retail and institutional interest has since tapered off, standing in sharp contrast to Ripple’s aggressive pursuit of enterprise partnerships aimed at deepening XRP’s cross-border payments ecosystem.

In recent months, XRP experienced a marked pullback, breaching the $1 support level in August this year. Despite this price stagnation, developer and institutional engagement across the XRP Ledger remains resilient. Furthermore, continued adoption by major financial conglomerates, such as Japan’s SBI Group, underscores the long-term staying power of the protocol.

Addressing how this growing enterprise footprint translates into structural demand for XRP, Odelia Torteman, head of digital assets at XRPL Commons, highlighted the ledger’s native architecture. She noted that features such as multi-purpose tokens, permissioned domains, and a permissioned decentralized exchange (DEX) support institutional requirements directly onchain, with XRP playing a core functional role.

“Accounts, and the objects they own on the ledger, such as trust lines, offers or escrows, require an XRP reserve. As the number of accounts and assets grows, so does the amount of XRP held for this purpose,” Torteman told Bitcoin.com News, adding that XRP also serves as a key bridge asset for liquidity across DEX routing and automated market maker pools.

Expanding on how emerging applications could generate durable demand, Torteman emphasized the ledger’s trajectory toward becoming a 24/7 compliance-grade settlement infrastructure for digital finance. As traditional finance and digital assets converge into “institutional DeFi,” she cited real-world asset (RWA) tokenization and stablecoin issuance as key drivers. The XRP Ledger ranks among the top three chains for RWAs, and Ripple’s stablecoin, RLUSD, surpassed $2 billion in market capitalization, with over half hosted on the XRPL.

“The next stage is credit on chain,” Torteman explained, noting that pending protocol activations like the Lending Protocol and Single Asset Vaults will enable underwritten, fixed-term credit models familiar to institutional allocators. “This is how a tokenised treasury becomes collateral, collateral becomes credit, and credit becomes structured yield, all on the same rail.”

Expanding Ecosystem via Cross-Chain Interoperability

Meanwhile, beyond native protocol expansion, cross-chain connectivity is emerging as another catalyst for ecosystem growth. Torteman highlighted the integration of the XRP Ledger into LOBSTR, an established wallet in the Stellar ecosystem, connecting two major payment-focused networks.

With the first phase live on iOS and Android, users can manage XRPL accounts, trade tokens on the native DEX, swap XRP across chains, and access fiat on-ramps for RLUSD. Torteman noted that value is actively moving between the two ecosystems, laying the foundation for the second phase, which will expand DeFi integrations and asset flows.

To translate these onchain capabilities into viable commercial products, XRPL Commons is targeting practical developer execution at its upcoming New York hackathon. Organized alongside industry partners including AWS, Mastercard, Ledger, and Quicknode, the event focuses on four core tracks, namely agentic finance, lending and borrowing, native protocol development, and an open innovation track.

Addressing the challenge of turning hackathon prototypes into lasting ventures, Torteman noted that top teams will receive technical mentorship, partner introductions, and access to dedicated startup programs. She highlighted that six teams from a previous buildathon in Paris have already launched businesses and joined XRPL startup pipelines.

title: USDC Network Fees in 2026: Ethereum vs Solana vs Other Chains, Priced to the Cent
summary: Ask three people what it costs to send USDC and you will get three answers. One says five dollars. One says a fraction of a cent. The third says it depends. The third person is right, and the reason is more interesting than it sounds.
content:
Skip to content

Ask three people what it costs to send USDC and you will get three answers. One says five dollars. One says a fraction of a cent. The third says it depends. The third person is right, and the reason is more interesting than it sounds.

A USDC balance is the same dollar on every chain Circle issues it on. Moving it is not the same price. In October 2026 the spread between the cheapest and the most expensive way to send $25 runs from well under a cent to a fifth of the deposit, and most of that gap has little to do with blockchain gas. This piece prices each network, shows where the money actually goes, and works out what a month of small transfers costs on each route.

Three charges hide inside one “network fee”

Every USDC transfer can carry up to three costs. The first is gas, paid to the network in its native coin: ETH on Ethereum and its rollups, SOL on Solana, POL on Polygon. The second is the platform fee charged by whatever sends the coin. Exchanges usually take a flat amount per withdrawal, and they set it, not the chain. The third is setup, either a one-time account charge on some chains or a bridge fee when the coin has to change networks first.

Wallet screens tend to show only the first. Exchange screens tend to show only the second. The total is what leaves your balance, and that is the number worth comparing.

Ethereum mainnet: cheap gas, expensive habits

Ethereum earned its reputation in 2021, when gas above 100 gwei turned a stablecoin transfer into a ten-dollar errand. That is not 2026. Average gas has sat well under 1 gwei for most of this year, around 0.1 gwei by mid-2026 on Spark’s tracking.

The math is short. A USDC transfer burns roughly 45,000 units of gas, closer to 65,000 when the receiving address has never held USDC. With ETH near $2,700 in early October:

  • At 0.1 gwei: about 1 to 2 cents
  • At 1 gwei: about 12 to 18 cents
  • At 10 gwei: about $1.22 to $1.76
  • At 40 gwei, a busy day by current standards: about $4.86 to $7.02

So why do comparison guides still quote $2 to $5 for Ethereum? Because that is close to what exchanges charge. One of the largest venues lists a $5 USDC withdrawal on Ethereum against $0.80 on Solana. Another charges $4 on Ethereum and $1 on most other networks. Those fees did not fall when gas did.

For usd coin gambling on a small bankroll, that distinction decides everything. Send from a self-custody wallet and Ethereum costs pocket change most days. Send straight from an exchange and the same chain can eat 20% of a $25 deposit.

Solana: a fraction of a cent, plus a one-time charge

Solana prices transactions another way. Each signature carries a fixed base fee of 5,000 lamports, or 0.000005 SOL, with an optional priority tip on top. With SOL around $121 on October 6, that is about six hundredths of a cent per transfer.

There is one wrinkle. Solana keeps token balances in separate accounts, and a wallet that has never held USDC needs one created before it can receive any. Creating it locks up about 0.00204 SOL as rent, roughly 25 cents today. The sender usually pays it, once. Close the account later and that deposit comes back.

Settlement is quick. Transfers confirm in well under a second and finalize in about 13 seconds.Solana also holds the second largest pool of native USDC, about $8.6 billion against Ethereum’s $51 billion as of April 2026, per Circle’s transparency figures. Depth matters because it decides where exchanges and wallets route USDC by default.

Base, Arbitrum, Polygon and the low-cost middle

Between those two sits a crowd of networks that settle USDC for a cent or two. Eco’s May 2026 survey puts typical transfer costs at:

  • Base: about $0.01
  • Polygon PoS: about $0.01
  • Avalanche: about $0.01
  • Optimism: about $0.02
  • Arbitrum One: about $0.05
  • Stellar: about $0.00001

Base, Arbitrum and Optimism are rollups. They borrow Ethereum’s security by posting batches back to the main chain, which is why a Base transfer looks done in about two seconds but only becomes final at the Ethereum level after roughly 15 minutes. For a deposit that gap rarely matters. For larger sums, it is why some platforms wait longer before crediting rollup transfers.

Exchange fees still apply here. A flat $1 withdrawal on Polygon or Arbitrum is a hundred times the gas, or twenty.

What a month of $25 deposits actually costs

Per-transfer comparisons hide the part that hurts: repetition. Take a player who tops up a usdc casino balance with eight $25 deposits over a month, $200 in all.

  • Exchange withdrawal on Ethereum at $5: $40, or 20% of the money moved
  • Exchange withdrawal on a rollup at $1: $8, or 4%
  • Exchange withdrawal on Solana at $0.80: $6.40, or 3.2%
  • Self-custody wallet on Ethereum at 1 gwei: about $1.40, or 0.7%
  • Self-custody wallet on Arbitrum: about 40 cents
  • Self-custody wallet on Base: about 8 cents
  • Self-custody wallet on Solana: under a cent, plus 25 cents once if the receiving account is new

Now set that against the games. Wager the whole $200 once on titles returning 98% and the expected cost of play is $4. The first route on that list costs ten times the house edge before a single bet is placed. The last costs nothing worth counting.

There is a fix simpler than switching chains. Batch. One $200 deposit on the priciest exchange route costs $5, or 2.5%. Eight small ones cost 20%.

Moving USDC between chains without a wrapped token

Sometimes the coin is simply on the wrong network. The clean route is Circle’s Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol, which burns USDC on one chain and mints native USDC on the other instead of handing over a wrapped IOU. CCTP V2 charges no protocol fee; you pay gas at both ends. Its standard lane takes 13 to 19 minutes, set by the source chain’s finality. A Fast Transfer lane finishes in about 20 seconds.

The source chain still writes the bill. Moving USDC from Ethereum to Solana runs roughly $3 to $6 in Eco’s estimate, nearly all of it on the Ethereum side.

Third-party bridges are easier to find and sometimes cheaper between rollups, often 0.10% to 0.20% on a $1,000 transfer. The catch is what arrives. A wrapped or bridged token is not always accepted where native USDC is, and that mismatch is how deposits go missing.

Tron and the networks USDC has left

Plenty of wallets still offer a USDC option on Tron. Treat it as legacy. Circle stopped minting USDC on Tron in February 2024 and ended transfer support for its business customers in February 2025, citing its risk framework. Older tokens still exist, liquidity has thinned, and a platform that takes USDC elsewhere may not credit a Tron transfer at all. Tron is the cheap home of USDT, not USDC. Confusing the two is common and expensive.

The same rule covers every chain in this piece. You must send on a network the destination accepts. A USDC transfer to the right address on the wrong chain is not delayed. It is usually gone, and no fee saving is worth that.

Picking a network before you send

A short checklist covers most of it:

  • Check which networks the receiving platform supports, on its deposit screen rather than an old help article.
  • Compare the full cost: gas, the sender’s withdrawal fee and any account setup.
  • Use self-custody or a fee-free route for small, frequent transfers.
  • Batch wherever the fee is flat.
  • Send a small test amount the first time you use a new route.

Gambling sites show why step one matters. The Jacks Club USDC casino page, for example, says USDC covers deposits, play and withdrawals across the site, that deposits credit once the network confirms them, and that supported networks and minimums are listed on the deposit screen rather than fixed in the page copy. That is the right instinct. Network support changes faster than marketing text does.

Before any coin moves, check that online gambling is legal where you live and that the site accepts players from your country. Then do the arithmetic. Fees are the cost of getting a dollar to the table; the house edge is the cost of playing it. Only one of those is fully in your hands, and on most routes in 2026 it can be pushed close to zero.

title: This Week in Crypto Law (October 18, 2026)
summary: Law and Ledger is a news segment focusing on crypto legal news, brought to you by Kelman Law – A law firm focused on digital asset commerce. The opinion editorial below was written by Michael Handelsman for Kelman.Law. This Week in Crypto Law This week’s developments show courts and regulators addre...
content:
Law and Ledger is a news segment focusing on crypto legal news, brought to you by Kelman Law – A law firm focused on digital asset commerce.

The opinion editorial below was written by Michael Handelsman for Kelman.Law.

This Week in Crypto Law

This week’s developments show courts and regulators addressing crypto through several distinct legal frameworks. A federal court declined to erase a settled CFTC enforcement case despite the agency’s change in policy. The OCC documented banking restrictions affecting digital-asset businesses, while litigation over Illinois’s unusual crypto transaction tax moved toward an expedited decision. In Europe, USDC became the first e-money token classified as significant under MiCA. A major English asset-recovery proceeding also produced an important choice-of-law ruling concerning 61,000 seized bitcoin.

Federal Court Refuses to Vacate the CFTC’s Gemini Settlement

On October 15, Judge Alvin Hellerstein of the Southern District of New York denied a joint request by the CFTC and Gemini Trust Company to vacate their January 2025 consent order.

The CFTC originally sued Gemini in 2022, alleging that the exchange made false or misleading statements during the agency’s review of a proposed bitcoin futures contract. Gemini later agreed to pay a $5 million civil penalty and accept a permanent injunction. Earlier this year, however, the CFTC joined Gemini in seeking relief from the judgment after concluding that the case would not have been filed under the agency’s current enforcement standards.

The court’s October 15 order declined to reopen the judgment. Judge Hellerstein found that the parties had not satisfied the standards for post-judgment relief. The CFTC’s revised policy position did not require vacatur, and Gemini had litigated the matter for more than three years before voluntarily settling shortly before trial. The $5 million penalty had already been paid, but the permanent injunction also remains in place.

The decision has significance beyond Gemini. A change in an agency’s leadership or enforcement priorities does not automatically unwind a final judicial order. Companies considering settlements should therefore assess the enduring consequences of injunctive language, admissions, undertakings and collateral regulatory effects. An agency’s later willingness to revisit a matter may not be enough if judicial approval is required.

OCC Report Finds Large Banks Restricted Digital-Asset Businesses

On October 14, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency released the results of its supervisory review of debanking practices at the nine largest national banks under its supervision.

The OCC’s report and accompanying announcement state that all nine banks maintained policies between 2020 and September 2025 that could restrict financial services based on lawful business activities or other nonfinancial considerations. The OCC specifically identified digital-asset issuers, exchanges and administrators among the industry sectors subject to restrictions.

The agency attributed many of the problems to broad reputational-risk policies that lacked objective, risk-based standards. The OCC reviewed approximately 50,000 documents totaling roughly 420,000 pages, along with nearly 100,000 complaints. It is now considering further changes to the regulatory and supervisory framework governing the largest banks.

The report does not itself create a new right to a bank account or prohibit banks from declining customers for legitimate financial-crime, credit or operational reasons. Banks still must manage sanctions, anti-money-laundering and other legal risks. The development is nevertheless important for crypto companies because it signals greater scrutiny of categorical exclusions and decisions that cannot be tied to documented risks.

Digital-asset businesses seeking banking relationships should be prepared to demonstrate their licensing position, transaction-monitoring controls, customer profile and approach to sanctions and fraud. Companies that lose banking services should also preserve communications identifying the bank’s stated reasons, especially where those reasons appear unrelated to the company’s actual risk profile.

Illinois Crypto Tax Litigation Moves Toward Expedited Resolution

On October 13, industry groups and the State of Illinois jointly asked the Circuit Court of Sangamon County to expedite two challenges to the state’s Digital Asset Tax Act.

The Act would impose a 0.2% tax on the value of specified digital-asset purchases and transfers. The pending lawsuits allege, among other things, violations of federal and state constitutional provisions and preemption by the federal Internet Tax Freedom Act. Those allegations have not yet been adjudicated.

According to the Crypto Council for Innovation’s filing announcement, the parties proposed that opening summary-judgment motions be filed on November 4, with briefing completed by January 22, 2027. They requested a February hearing and a decision by March 1. The proposed schedule still requires court approval. Enforcement of the tax has separately been stayed until July 1, 2027.

The new development is procedural rather than a ruling on the tax’s legality. Nevertheless, the stay provides additional preparation time, and the requested schedule could produce a merits decision before the revised effective date.

Exchanges, brokers and other businesses with Illinois customers should not treat the delay as invalidation of the law. They should continue evaluating whether the Act would cover their transactions, who would be responsible for collection and how their systems would calculate the tax if the challenges fail.

EBA Classifies USDC as the EU’s First Significant E-Money Token

On October 14, the European Banking Authority classified USDC as the first “significant” e-money token under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation.

The EBA’s announcement states that 45 e-money tokens have been notified under MiCA, but USDC is the first to meet the applicable significance criteria. Circle Internet Financial Europe SAS issues USDC in the European Union.

Beginning November 12, USDC will be subject to MiCA’s dual-supervision model for significant e-money tokens. The EBA will assume direct responsibility for areas including own funds, reserve assets, liquidity requirements, and recovery and redemption planning. France’s Autorité de Contrôle Prudentiel et de Résolution will retain responsibility for governance, outsourcing, qualifying holdings, conflicts of interest and fitness assessments.

This is materially different from last week’s ESMA opinion concerning stablecoins that do not comply with MiCA. The EBA’s decision does not identify USDC as noncompliant. Instead, it subjects USDC to heightened supervision because of its scale and importance.

The classification matters not only to Circle. Exchanges, custodians and payment businesses using USDC should expect more formalized supervisory coordination and potentially more detailed operational requests concerning reserve, redemption and liquidity arrangements. Other stablecoin issuers approaching the significance thresholds should study the allocation of responsibilities between the EBA and their national regulator.

English Court Applies Chinese Law to Claims Over 61,000 Seized Bitcoin

On October 12, the High Court in London ruled that Chinese law governs fraud victims’ ownership claims to approximately 61,000 bitcoin seized by British authorities.

The bitcoin is connected to Zhimin Qian, who was convicted following a large investment fraud conducted in China. Victims argued that English property law should govern because the bitcoin is held in the United Kingdom. Mr. Justice Mark Turner instead concluded that Chinese law applies because the alleged misrepresentations, transfers of money, contractual relationships and immediate economic losses occurred in China.

The ruling does not decide who ultimately owns the bitcoin. The claimants must now establish relevant property rights under Chinese law and show that those rights satisfy the United Kingdom’s requirements for returning seized criminal property. A further hearing is expected, and the claimants have indicated that they intend to appeal.

For cross-border crypto asset recovery, the decision underscores that the physical or technical location of seized assets may not determine the law governing competing ownership claims. Courts may instead focus on where the underlying fraud, payment and economic loss occurred. Victims pursuing recovery should develop their choice-of-law analysis early and obtain appropriate foreign-law evidence rather than assuming that seizure in a favorable jurisdiction will determine ownership.

Businesses and individuals assessing regulatory, litigation, tax or digital-asset recovery issues arising from these developments may contact Kelman PLLC to discuss their circumstances.

TL;DR: Research attributed to Castle Labs puts Solana’s real-world asset market at about $4.3 billion, versus $700 million a year earlier. Ethereum remains substantially larger, but the gap has narrowed sharply.

Solana’s next growth story may have less to do with meme coins and more to do with assets that already exist in the traditional financial system.

According to a recent Castle Labs assessment of the ecosystem, the value of real-world assets represented on Solana rose from approximately $700 million to $4.3 billion over twelve months. That is more than a sixfold increase in the market’s size, although it should not be confused with a 600% mathematical gain: the increase from those rounded figures is about 514%.

The comparison with Ethereum is revealing. The same report put Ethereum’s tokenized asset value at roughly $16.6 billion, against $15.5 billion a year earlier. Ethereum remains almost four times Solana’s size by this measure, but Solana’s total now equals about 26% of Ethereum’s, up from approximately 4.5%.

The category includes assets such as tokenized securities, credit and yield-bearing instruments, rather than a single kind of token. The figures can shift as new products are issued, underlying market values move and data providers change how they categorize assets.

It is tempting to treat the increase as a direct forecast for SOL’s price, but that leap would be unjustified. Tokenization can grow without every dollar of additional asset value translating neatly into demand for a network’s native token.

The more useful conclusion is that Solana is becoming a meaningful venue for financial instruments beyond cryptocurrencies themselves. Whether it can close more of the gap with Ethereum will depend on issuers, liquidity and the quality of the applications built around those assets.

title: Thai Police Bust Chinese Boss Behind $74M Crypto Laundering Ring
summary: Thai Immigration Police arrested Wu Chaoshuai, a Chinese national who had entered the country on a tourist visa back in 2019, and had taken action to evade arrest. Chaoshuai allegedly led a cryptocurrency laundering ring that moved over $74 million for a transnational criminal organization. Chinese ...
content:
Thai Immigration Police arrested Wu Chaoshuai, a Chinese national who had entered the country on a tourist visa back in 2019, and had taken action to evade arrest. Chaoshuai allegedly led a cryptocurrency laundering ring that moved over $74 million for a transnational criminal organization.

Key Takeaways

  • Thai police arrested a Chinese kingpin accused of using crypto exchanges to launder over $74M.
  • The suspect used fake IDs, altered cars, and frequent moves to evade arrest after overstaying his visa.
  • Thailand will charge and extradite him, marking another crackdown on regional crypto-linked money laundering.

Chinese Crypto Money Laundering Kingpin Arrested in Thailand

Thai authorities announced the arrest of a money laundering kingpin who fled China to avoid arrest and remained in the country after his visa expired.

An investigation that encompassed the actions of several Thai immigration police officials has concluded with the arrest of Wu Chaoshuai, a Chinese national who allegedly managed a transnational criminal organization that used cryptocurrency for money laundering purposes.

Chinese authorities allege Wu served as an account mule for the organization, hiring other people to open bank accounts and cryptocurrency exchanges to obscure and facilitate the movement of illicit funds. Wu managed 133 accounts and reportedly processed over $74 million in transactions.

According to the third division of the Thai Immigration police, Wu entered Thailand using a tourist visa in December 2019 and remained after its expiry, likely to avoid leaving and being detected by Immigration authorities, which could arrange his extradition to China.

To avoid being tracked by Thai authorities, Wu moved across the country, avoiding staying in just one location for an extended period. The Thai press reported that Wu moved between various residences frequently, renting houses and luxury condos in different communities. Similarly, Wu also changed his car color and used fake license plates and forged documents to throw authorities off his track.

Nonetheless, Thai police found that Wu was hiding in a luxury house in the Ramkhamhaeng area in Bangkok. At the time of his arrest, Wu’s visa had expired over three years ago.

Wu will be charged with remaining in Thailand after his visa expired, and Thai police will coordinate his extradition with Chinese authorities.

Thai authorities have strengthened their oversight of cryptocurrency movements and crimes. In June, the Department of Special Investigation dismantled a crypto mining money laundering organization that laundered over $300 million annually from online scams and gambling platforms.

TL;DR: Sazmining is offering individual Proto immersion hashboards at $4,187 each, with financing and managed hosting. The arrangement lowers the upfront hardware purchase but does not remove Bitcoin mining‘s ongoing costs or profitability risk.

Buying into industrial Bitcoin mining usually means dealing with noisy equipment, electricity contracts and cooling infrastructure. A new offering built around Block’s Proto hardware takes a different approach: purchase a single hashboard and leave the hosting to someone else.

Sazmining lists Proto immersion hashboards configured for approximately 204 terahashes per second, with efficiency of roughly 15 joules per terahash. Three boards make up a full Proto Immersion Module, but customers can start with one.

The advertised hardware price is $4,187. Its financing option requires $1,397 upfront followed by 18 monthly payments of $155, at a stated 0% interest rate. A separate hosting and maintenance fee of $153 a month applies, covering power at the quoted service rate and operational support.

Those recurring charges are central to the economics. A lower entry price does not mean free mining, and the Bitcoin received depends on network difficulty, rewards, uptime, fees and the market price of BTC. A hashboard can be technically efficient and still produce disappointing returns for its owner.

For Block, the offer broadens the potential audience for its Proto equipment. For Sazmining, it packages industrial hardware into a managed service that customers can purchase in smaller units.

The appeal is convenience and modularity. The question for buyers is whether the projected mining revenue comfortably covers all the costs that continue after the hardware purchase.

title: A Missouri Woman Felt Jealous When She Heard About a $228,000 Jackpot. Then She Checked Her Own Ticket
summary: A Missouri Lottery player in Arnold matched all five numbers in the Aug. 10, 2026 Show Me Cash drawing to win a $228,000 jackpot on a ticket bought at the Circle K on Jeffco Blvd. Before realizing it was her, she saw a sign touting a local winner and felt a twinge of jealousy, then […]
content:
A Missouri Lottery player in Arnold matched all five numbers in the Aug. 10, 2026 Show Me Cash drawing to win a $228,000 jackpot on a ticket bought at the Circle K on Jeffco Blvd. Before realizing it was her, she saw a sign touting a local winner and felt a twinge of jealousy, then checked her own numbers and discovered the prize.

Key Takeaways

  • A Missouri Lottery player in Arnold matched all five numbers (4, 12, 23, 24, 37) in the Aug. 10, 2026 Show Me Cash drawing to win a $228,000 jackpot on a ticket from the Circle K at 504 Jeffco Blvd.
  • She saw a sign announcing a local winner and felt “a twinge of jealousy” before checking her own ticket and discovering the prize was hers.
  • The anonymous winner put part of the money into retirement savings and plans to use some as a down payment on a house.

A sign in Arnold, Missouri, touted a $228,000 Show Me Cash jackpot winner, and one local player felt “a twinge of jealousy,” the Missouri Lottery said. “I was like, ‘God, why couldn’t that be me?’” she recalled, before doing what most lottery players do next: checking her own numbers. They matched all five from the 8/10/2026 drawing, 4, 12, 23, 24, and 37, on a ticket bought at the Circle K at 504 Jeffco Blvd. By the time the story hit Fox2Now on 9/29/2026 and Lottery Post on 10/2/2026, the anonymous winner said she’d already put some of the money toward retirement and was eyeing a down payment on a house.

An unexpected turn for a convenience-store regular

Sometimes the most American tech story is hiding in plain sight, right next to the coffee machine. A lottery ticket is still a paper slip, but it rides on a statewide system of terminals, nightly draws, and instant verification. In Arnold, Missouri, one player learned that firsthand after landing the $228,000 Show Me Cash jackpot in August.

The Missouri Lottery said the winning ticket came from a Circle K at 504 Jeffco Blvd in Arnold. The prize traced back to the August 10, 2026 drawing, when her ticket matched all 5 numbers: 4, 12, 23, 24, and 37, as detailed in the Lottery Post report.

“Why couldn’t that be me?” (It was.)

Before she checked her ticket, the winner walked past a sign announcing that someone in town had hit Show Me Cash and felt, as the lottery put it, a “twinge of jealousy.” “I was like, ‘God, why couldn’t that be me?’” she said. Then the mundane act that makes modern lotteries work, verifying numbers, flipped the whole day: “I check my numbers and… yeah, I won.”

The state later leaned into the irony with an official news release titled “$228,000 Jackpot Winner Jealous of Her Own Win,” dated September 25, 2026, posted on the Missouri Lottery News Releases page.

A Missouri-only game, built for habit

Show Me Cash is a Missouri-exclusive daily draw, a smaller and more frequent rhythm than national brands. Jackpots start at $50,000 and grow until someone wins, with drawings held nightly at approximately 8:59 p.m. Central Time. The winner told the lottery she sticks to this local pattern: “I tell everybody I don’t play Powerball or Mega Millions.”

That kind of loyalty is also a distribution story: a game designed to be purchased alongside gas and snacks, validated quickly, and talked about on local signage that can nudge someone to pull out a ticket and re-check.

Turning a windfall into a balance sheet

By the time the story hit wider circulation, the winner was already treating the payout like personal finance, not fantasy. “I’m trying to be responsible with it,” she said, explaining that she had put some of the $228,000 into retirement savings and planned to use some as a down payment on a house.

Her name was not released, and coverage including Fox2Now’s September 29, 2026 story kept her anonymous. For a system built on publicity, it was a quiet ending, and a very practical one.

TL;DR: Stock-linked tokens deployed in DeFi reached an estimated $262.4 million across blockchains at the end of September, up nearly 18-fold from the start of 2026. Base accounted for about $16 million, not the entire total.

Tokenized stocks are starting to do more than sit in digital wallets. A September 30 snapshot put approximately $262.4 million of stock-linked assets into decentralized finance applications across multiple blockchains, compared with around $14.66 million at the beginning of the year.

The figures describe assets being used in DeFi, not the total value of all tokenized equities outstanding. That distinction is important as the category grows more complicated, with different issuers, networks and financial rights behind products that can look similar on a trading screen.

Solana accounted for about $95.9 million of the DeFi amount in the tracked figures, while Robinhood Chain held approximately $79.9 million. Base’s reported portion was closer to $16 million. The growth story, in other words, is spread across several networks rather than belonging exclusively to one exchange or Layer 2.

Once stock-linked tokens can be exchanged in automated markets or pledged as collateral, investors gain new ways to put positions to work. The trade-off is exposure to protocol risks and liquidity conditions that do not exist in the same form in an ordinary brokerage account.

It is also important not to assume that every token represents direct legal ownership of an underlying share. Rights, redemption mechanisms and eligibility rules vary by issuer.

The $262 million figure is still small beside conventional equity markets. But its significance lies in what those assets are being used for: programmable financial activity, not simply a blockchain-branded way to hold a stock.

title: A $98 Million Bitcoin Long Bet on Hyperliquid Hangs by a Thin Thread
summary: A bitcoin trader is staring down a potential $98 million liquidation after a punishing week wiped nearly $9.8 million from a Hyperliquid account. With 40x leverage and bitcoin’s price slipping toward $81,000, another sharp decline could finish the job. Hyperliquid Trader Risks $98 Million Bitcoin Li...
content:
A bitcoin trader is staring down a potential $98 million liquidation after a punishing week wiped nearly $9.8 million from a Hyperliquid account. With 40x leverage and bitcoin’s price slipping toward $81,000, another sharp decline could finish the job.

Key Takeaways

  • A Hyperliquid trader holds a $97.87 million bitcoin long with 40x isolated leverage.
  • Bitcoin’s price traded near $81,117 on Bitstamp at 12:30 p.m., just 1.59% above the trader’s estimated liquidation price.
  • Hyperliquid account data shows nearly $9.8 million in weekly losses and a 16.67% win rate.

Hyperliquid Trader Risks $98 Million Bitcoin Liquidation

A massive bitcoin long position on Hyperliquid is teetering dangerously close to liquidation, with its owner controlling 1,205.30865 BTC worth approximately $97.87 million. The position carries 40x isolated leverage, leaving precious little room for another market stumble.

The trader entered at an average bitcoin price of $81,913.80, but bitcoin’s retreat has already inflicted an unrealized loss of $866,467.24, translating into a negative 30.4% return on equity (ROE). Worse still, the position’s estimated liquidation price sits at $79,828.

The account holds approximately $2.91 million in equity, with $2.85 million committed as margin. Its effective leverage ratio stands at 34.33x, while available margin has dwindled to zero. Funding costs have also extracted $86,952.49 from the position.

Bitcoin Price Slides as Selling Pressure Intensifies

Sunday’s market action hasn’t offered much comfort. Bitcoin climbed to $82,170 earlier in the session before sellers seized control, driving the cryptocurrency to an intraday low of $80,888. At approximately 12:25 p.m. EDT on Oct. 18, bitcoin traded near $81,117 on Bitstamp, leaving the trader’s liquidation threshold roughly $1,289 away, a distance of just 1.59%.

Short-term BTC/USD charts capture the damage. Successive red candles battered bitcoin below $81,800, $81,400, and $81,200, accompanied by heavier trading volume during the sharpest declines. Buyers have since attempted to defend $81,000, but the recovery remains tentative. A renewed break beneath $80,888 would put additional pressure on the trader’s already strained position.

Nearly $9.8 Million Lost in One Week

The perps DEX account’s recent trading record tells an even harsher story. Over seven days, its cumulative profit and loss plunged to negative $9,779,348.87, while its weekly maximum drawdown reached 78.77%. Across 3,763 recorded trades, hyperbot.network data shows a win rate of just 16.67%. The trader remains entirely exposed to bitcoin’s upside, with 100% long exposure and no short positions providing a counterweight.

Interestingly, bitcoin doesn’t need to crash for this trade to go off the rails. A relatively ordinary market decline could push the position into liquidation territory. There is one important distinction. The $97.87 million figure represents leveraged exposure, not the trader’s personal capital at risk. Actual liquidation depends on Hyperliquid’s mark price and margin calculations, and forced liquidation could occur in stages.

For now, nearly $98 million in bitcoin exposure rests on a margin cushion that could disappear with another difficult afternoon.

TL;DR: Fidelity’s technology research team says Solana has operated for more than two years without a major mainnet outage, while maintaining roughly 99.7% vote success. It also warns that validator and infrastructure concentration remain important concerns.

Solana’s reputation was once shaped by how often the network stopped. A new assessment from Fidelity’s Center for Applied Technology shows how much that conversation has changed, without claiming the engineering risks have disappeared.

Published October 16, the research highlights more than two years of operation without a major mainnet outage and a vote success rate of approximately 99.7%. Those measures point to a network that has become more dependable as the financial activity running across it has grown.

The stakes are rising. Fidelity’s researchers note that Solana has handled substantial stablecoin activity and is attracting tokenized assets and institutional participation. A fast chain becomes a very different proposition when users depend on it for more than short-lived speculative trades.

Yet the report does not hand the network an unqualified clean bill of health. Stake concentration, hosting dependencies, software-client diversity and the geographic distribution of infrastructure all influence whether a chain can withstand a serious disruption.

Solana is pursuing further performance improvements, including shorter slot times and new software clients. Those efforts may raise capacity, but raw speed is only one part of network resilience. It also matters how many independent participants can keep a system functioning if a major operator or piece of infrastructure fails.

Fidelity’s central message is less about celebrating a benchmark than about asking a tougher question: can Solana preserve decentralization and reliability as more consequential financial activity arrives?
